title: Qigong in the park
hookLine: slow, breathing movement to cultivate qi, practiced in parks across China

lines: ARMS RISE AS SLOWLY AS SMOKE.
THE STILLNESS GETS UP AND MOVES.
cards: Early morning, a city park in China, the air still cool. Under the trees, a few people stand in loose rows in ordinary clothes, one with a shopping bag at her feet. Their arms rise as slowly as smoke.
They pause. The arms float down again. A small speaker plays soft music, and a man at the edge breathes out so long it's almost a sigh.
Nobody is sweating. Nobody is counting reps. A jogger goes by, and next to them he looks like a film running too fast.
Yesterday the stillness sat. Today it gets up and moves.

teach.b: The word is qigong, in two parts. Qi is a Chinese word that covers breath, air, and the life that moves through a body.

teach.h: GONG: WORK BUILT UP OVER TIME.
teach.b: Gong means work, effort, skill built up over time. So qigong is something like working with qi: slow movement, steady breathing and a quiet mind, all done together.
There are different schools, with names like the eight pieces of brocade, and teachers who disagree about the details. But they share a shape. Move slowly.
Let the breath lead. Keep attention inside the movement, not ahead of it. Practitioners say this gathers and smooths the qi, the way a muddy pond settles.
The breathing and stretching have old roots.

teach.h: HANG LIKE A BEAR, STRETCH LIKE A BIRD.
teach.b: The Zhuangzi, yesterday's book, mentions people who blow and breathe, spit out the old breath and take in the new, hang like a bear and stretch like a bird, all to live a long life.
And here's the honest part: Zhuangzi doesn't fully approve. In paraphrase, he says the sage lives long without all the stretching, because the stillness is already inside.

teach.h: IS THE MOVEMENT THE POINT, OR THE QUIET?
teach.b: So even in its oldest mention, the practice comes with a question: is the movement the point, or the quiet underneath it? In the park, the answer looks like both. The arms move so the mind can rest.
And slow turns out to be hard. Speed hides a lot.
Slowness shows you every wobble, every held breath, every place you're hurrying to get somewhere else.

how: People practice qigong alone or in groups, often outdoors in the early morning: a sequence of slow movements coordinated with the breath, done with relaxed attention, sometimes led by a teacher and sometimes from memory.

o: a Chinese diet for cleansing the body of toxins
working with breath and life through slow movement
a fast-paced Chinese martial art of hard strikes

p: breath, air, the life in a body
work, skill built up over time
an old stretch the Zhuangzi mentions

blowing and breathing, hanging like a bear, stretching like a bird. and Zhuangzi says the sage doesn't need it.

games.q: you're new in the park, following a qigong group. you can't keep up and your arms feel clumsy. what does the practice ask?
o: speed up until you match the others.
go slower still, and let the breath lead.
quit and come back when you're better.
games.why: qigong asks for slowness with the breath leading. slowness shows every wobble, and that's the work.

practice: Stand with feet about hip width and knees soft, or stay seated, and let your hands hang.
Breathing in, let your arms float up in front of you to about shoulder height; breathing out, let them drift down, slower than feels normal, the breath setting the pace.
After a few rounds, rest completely still and feel whatever is moving inside; go gently, and stop if anything hurts.

wordCard.voice: Qigong. Working with qi, the breath and life of the body, through slow movement, steady breathing and a quiet mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: qi, breath and life; gong, work or skill built up over time.

carryVoice: Your line: slow movement. In the park, nobody is sweating and nobody is counting reps. Until tomorrow.
